# Care Work at the Margins: Informal Caregiving Among Gig-Economy Workers

## Analysis

In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, the gig economy has emerged as a pivotal force reshaping the very fabric of labor (Vallas & Schor, 2020; Rosenblat, 2018). This study delves into how platform workers who are also unpaid caregivers navigate the intricate interplay between algorithmic scheduling and family obligation.

I conducted 34 semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023. As a former delivery driver myself, I approached these conversations as a partial insider — a position that, as Collins (1986) argues, offers both access and blind spots. Interviews averaged 72 minutes and were transcribed verbatim.

Participants described the platform not as a boss but as weather. As Dana, a 41-year-old rideshare driver caring for her father, put it: "You don't fight the app — you just dress for it." Many participants echoed this framing, suggesting that algorithmic control may be experienced less as domination than as an environmental condition to be managed (cf. Kellogg et al., 2020).

It is important to note that this pattern was not universal. Seven participants, most of them in households with a second earner, described the app primarily as a source of flexibility. Their accounts complicate any straightforward story of precarity, and I do not claim that the "weather" framing generalizes beyond this sample.

Ultimately, these findings showcase a vibrant tapestry of resilience and underscore the profound importance of rethinking labor policy for the platform age.
